item.text: I’ll read the five parts in order, place each new note in the map, then write the JSONL file and run the checker.

item.aggregated_output:
<<11:114 update 1, part 0 of 0..4>>
## THE CURRENT MAP
11:114/q01 What does it mean to establish prayer? [وَأَقِمِ ٱلصَّلَوٰةَ · interpretation]
  11:114/q01/p1 Perform the prescribed prayers fully, with their required acts and at their appointed times. — reasons: Al-Tabrisi and Ibn al-Jawzi specify complete bowing and prostration. Alusi includes regular observance or prayer at the beginning of its time. Jishumi says the verse fixes times generally while the Prophet explained details; Asad and Qurtubi likewise refer forms and exact times to prophetic teaching.
  11:114/q01/p2 Maintain prayer continuously, evenly, or at its best times. — reasons: These are alternative glosses reported by al-Tabrisi and Abu Hayyan; al-Alusi also reports regular maintenance and beginning-of-time performance.
  11:114/q01/p3 Fill one's time with obligatory and voluntary worship or remembrance. — reasons: Sufi authorities take the command to cover all time. Asad extends its stress on prayer to remembrance throughout waking life. Bursevi allows work, human needs, and restorative sleep.
  11:114/q01/p4 The five prayers close the five sensory doors and restore presence with God. — reasons: Qashani says the senses veil the heart; praying at day edges preserves gathered light through intervening times (23:9), while night wakefulness refines powers drawn toward sleep.
  11:114/q01/p5 Prayer is the foremost worship after faith and a refuge in hardship. — reasons: Razi relates its placement after steadfastness to its rank; Biqai calls it the broadest aid to uprightness; Qurtubi reports the Prophet turned to prayer when troubled.
11:114/q02 Which prayers are at the two ends of the day? [طَرَفَىِ ٱلنَّهَارِ · referent] (turns on: Whether dawn and sunset count within daytime, and whether the latter half of the day can contain both Zuhr and Asr as an end.)
  11:114/q02/p1 Fajr at the first end and Zuhr and Asr at the second. — reasons: Wahidi prefers Zajjaj: Maghrib belongs to night. Zamakhshari calls Zuhr and Asr evening prayers; Elmalili calls them the after-noon division. Tabatabai says the five-prayer report points to before and after noon. Qurtubi reports Ibn Atiyya's choice. Ibn al-Jawzi reports al-Dahhak accepts all three second-end views.
  11:114/q02/p2 Fajr and Asr. — reasons: Razi says sunrise and sunset mark opposite edges, leaving Maghrib to night; he parallels 20:130. Abu Hayyan says each boundary belongs to what it bounds and cites fasting from dawn. Biqai notes morning and afternoon prayer before the Night Journey. Ibn al-Jawzi reports al-Dahhak accepts all three second-end views. Razi says Abu Hanifa inferred later performance of Fajr and Asr near the boundaries.
  11:114/q02/p3 Fajr and Maghrib. — reasons: Tabari argues that all agree on Fajr and that Maghrib alone supplies the opposite end; Wahidi says the apparent wording supports it. Tabrisi says Zuhr and Asr are obvious daytime prayers or specified by 17:78. Qurtubi defends dawn as daytime from fasting law but retains the sunset objection. Kuranyolu defines day as dawn to sunset. Ibn al-Jawzi reports al-Dahhak accepts all three second-end views.
  11:114/q02/p4 Zuhr and Asr are the two boundaries; Fajr is grouped with night prayers. — reasons: Some connect this grouping with quiet versus loud recitation. Elmalili argues dawn is the day's root and noon and afternoon its two prominent parts; the night set of Maghrib, Isha and Fajr gives five prayers, with 17:78 and 20:130.
  11:114/q02/p5 Fajr and Isha. — reasons: Ibn Abi Hatim reports this from Mujahid.
  11:114/q02/p6 Fajr and Zuhr at one end, Asr and Maghrib at the other. — reasons: Wahidi and Baghawi attribute this division to Muqatil.
  11:114/q02/p7 The first end is Fajr, while the evening end remains disputed. — reasons: Tabari says all agree on Fajr but differ about evening; Ibn al-Jawzi reports the majority agrees, but notes Ibn Jarir gives Zuhr instead. Qurtubi transmits Mawardi's claimed agreement and qualifies it by the Zuhr/Asr view. Asad gives the literal wording, 'the two ends of the day.'
11:114/q03 Why is the yāʾ of طرفي pronounced with a vowel? [طَرَفَىِ ٱلنَّهَارِ · grammar]
  11:114/q03/p1 It meets a following still consonant and takes the usual kasra. — reasons: Akhfash compares صاحبي السجن at 12:39.
11:114/q04 Does avoiding major sins already require performing the five prayers? [ٱلسَّيِّـَٔاتِ · law]
  11:114/q04/p1 Yes, because abandoning prayer is a major sin. — reasons: Ibn Hajar argues this; al-Alusi says it merits examination.
11:114/q05 How does al-Tirmidhi grade the principal confession reports? [* · reports]
  11:114/q05/p1 The Ibn Masud account is hasan sahih; the Muadh and Abu al-Yusr routes are weak. — reasons: Ibn Ashur reports al-Tirmidhi's distinctions.
11:114/q06 Can night prayer erase sins committed during the day? [زُلَفًۭا مِّنَ ٱلَّيْلِ ٱلسَّيِّـَٔاتِ · interpretation]
  11:114/q06/p1 Yes, a believer's night prayer removes daytime sins. — reasons: Tabatabai cites Abu Abdillah and notes parallel transmissions in several collections.
11:114/q07 What does زلفا mean? [زُلَفًۭا · meaning]
  11:114/q07/p1 Near or successive hours, stages, or portions of the night; singular zulfa. — reasons: Akhfash lists zulfat and zulf as other plurals. Layth and Thalab specify the first night hours; Abu Ubayda, Akhfash and Ibn Qutayba allow any hour. Al-Ajjaj's poem uses successive zulf. Ibn Qutayba and Abu Hayyan derive nearness; Tabari and Mawardi give Muzdalifa etymologies, while Raghib includes rank, favor and euphemistic punishment. Zajjaj rejects an unattested night meaning for zalif.
11:114/q08 How is زلفا read? [زُلَفًۭا · readings] (turns on: The vowel on lam and whether the form is a plural, collective, or singular.)
  11:114/q08/p1 Zulafan, with damma on zay and fatha on lam, a plural of zulfa. — reasons: Tabari prefers this because Isha follows portions of the night; Sam in calls it the common reading, and Qurtubi and Abu Hayyan the majority reading.
  11:114/q08/p2 Zulufan, with damma on both letters. — reasons: Attributed to Medinan readers, Abu Jafar, Ibn Abi Ishaq, Talha and others. Analyses include a plural with vowel harmony, plural of zalif, or dialectal singular; Qiraat-ER says the plural pattern changes without changing meaning.
  11:114/q08/p3 Zulfan, with silent lam. — reasons: Attributed to some Meccan readers and to Ibn Muhaysin and Mujahid. It may shorten the vowelled form or function as a collective singular.
  11:114/q08/p4 Zulfa or zulfa, a singular near interval or rank. — reasons: Mujahid and Ibn Muhaysin transmit the feminine fuʿla form; Kashshaf compares qurba; Sam in calls it a singular adjective for a near rank or hour.
11:114/q09 How do طرفي النهار and زلفا function grammatically? [طَرَفَىِ ٱلنَّهَارِ زُلَفًۭا مِّنَ ٱلَّيْلِ · grammar] (turns on: Whether زلفا names a time coordinate with the day ends or a prayer coordinate with الصلاة.)
  11:114/q09/p1 Both are accusative time expressions governed by establish; زلفا is coordinated with طرفي. — reasons: Kashshaf, Nasafi and Sam in say taraf becomes temporal through annexation to a time, as do 'beginning of day' and 'half of night'; Sam in prefers governance by أقم.
  11:114/q09/p2 The night expressions are prayers that draw one near to God and coordinate with الصلاة. — reasons: Kashshaf supplies the alternative parsing as devotional night prayers; Sam in and Abu Hayyan report it.
  11:114/q09/p3 من الليل modifies زلفا as an adjective. — reasons: Sam in explicitly parses the prepositional phrase as a qualifier.
11:114/q10 Which prayers are meant by the night intervals? [زُلَفًۭا مِّنَ ٱلَّيْلِ · referent] (turns on: Which hours count as night approaches and whether the plural requires at least three prayers.)
  11:114/q10/p1 Maghrib and Isha. — reasons: Hasan transmits this as the Prophet's description of two night intervals; Tabari lists early authorities. Zajjaj and Wahidi put sunset within night.
  11:114/q10/p2 Isha alone, in a later portion of night. — reasons: Mujahid calls it an hour at Isha. Ibn Abbas cited the phrase in favor of delaying Isha; Tabari says Isha follows portions of night.
  11:114/q10/p3 Voluntary night vigil or tahajjud. — reasons: Ibn Abi Hatim reports Ibn Abbas's voluntary-night gloss. Ibn Kathir describes the earlier obligation of night vigil and its later abrogation; Bursevi cites 17:79 for the Prophet.
  11:114/q10/p4 Maghrib, Isha, and Fajr. — reasons: The dawn-as-night classification may follow loud recitation; Elmalili argues this yields five prayers.
  11:114/q10/p5 Maghrib, Isha, and witr or night vigil; or Isha, witr, and tahajjud. — reasons: Razi and Elmalili infer at least three from the broken plural; Razi argues witr obligation using 34:20, while Elmalili describes a possible sixth prayer and 17:79. Bursevi reports Abu Hanifa's witr view.
  11:114/q10/p6 Night prayer without specifying which one. — reasons: Qurtubi attributes this to Akhfash.
11:114/q11 What do the prayer times establish as a legal duty? [وَأَقِمِ ٱلصَّلَوٰةَ طَرَفَىِ ٱلنَّهَارِ وَزُلَفًۭا مِّنَ ٱلَّيْلِ · law] (turns on: Whether the plural of night intervals denotes specific obligatory prayers and how much detail the verse itself supplies.)
  11:114/q11/p1 They indicate the five obligatory prayers, while prophetic practice supplies their exact times and form. — reasons: Qurtubi cites 16:44 and other prayer verses, the Prophet's 'pray as you have seen me pray,' and completion of religion at 5:3. Elmalili infers five from two day periods and three night periods.
  11:114/q11/p2 Only two daily prayers are obligatory. — reasons: The Kharijites construe the night phrase as an adjective to the day ends and argue the two prayers erase even omission of other prayers.
  11:114/q11/p3 Witr is obligatory as a third night prayer. — reasons: Razi invokes the plural minimum of three and 34:20; Bursevi cites Abu Hanifa; Elmalili says a sixth prayer is probable, so witr is practical wājib rather than a creed obligation.
  11:114/q11/p4 Five established prayers ar

<<11:114 update 1, part 1 of 0..4>>
e performed in congregation. — reasons: Elmalili says the call is sunnah and congregational prayer wājib.
11:114/q12 What are the good deeds that remove bad deeds? [ٱلْحَسَنَٰتِ · referent] (turns on: Whether the definite good deeds refer to the preceding prayer, particular devotions, or the general class of obedience.)
  11:114/q12/p1 The five prescribed prayers, especially with ablution. — reasons: Tabari prefers this from context and recurrent sound prophetic reports; Ibn al-Jawzi prefers the majority and a connected report. Ka'b, Salman and the Prophet compare prayer to washing dirt or shaking leaves; Uthman says each prayer expiates the interval since the prior prayer.
  11:114/q12/p2 All acts of obedience or accepted good deeds, with prayer as a leading example. — reasons: Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan treat specific deeds as examples of general wording. Alusi adduces reports on voluntary affirmation, fasting Arafat, and gratitude. Qushayri lists nearness, remorse, tears, kindness, generosity, good opinion, sincerity and truthfulness as remedies for particular faults. Bursevi ranks knowledge of God, monotheism and resisting the lower self highly.
  11:114/q12/p3 Remembrance formulas: glorification, praise, testimony of divine unity, and magnification. — reasons: Most reports attribute these to Mujahid, with slight variation: Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu Hayyan include reliance on God; Ata calls them the enduring good works. Abu Dharr's report calls the testimony the best good deed; Bursevi transmits the same answer from the Prophet.
  11:114/q12/p4 Repentance and return to obedience. — reasons: Jishumi prefers Abu Ali's reading: unbelievers can do good without erasure, so repentance is essential; Tabrisi says repentance certainly cancels punishment.
  11:114/q12/p5 The Prophet's and believers' good actions that overcome polytheists' evil actions. — reasons: This interpretation makes the verse a promise of religious victory; Abu Muslim links it to truth crushing falsehood in 21:18.
11:114/q13 How do good deeds remove bad deeds? [إِنَّ ٱلْحَسَنَٰتِ يُذْهِبْنَ ٱلسَّيِّـَٔاتِ · interpretation] (turns on: Whether removal means retrospective expiation, prevention of future wrongdoing, or spiritual transformation.)
  11:114/q13/p1 They expiate the guilt, punishment, or effects of earlier sins. — reasons: Abu Hayyan and Bursevi distinguish expiation from making a past act never occur. Alusi says liability is removed; another explanation has records erased. Tabatabai speaks of traces in believers' souls. Ibn Kathir cites ablution and two-unit prayer reports.
  11:114/q13/p2 Regular good deeds help a person stop committing sins. — reasons: Al-Asamm, Kashshaf, Abu Hayyan and Bursevi cite prayer restraining indecency at 29:45; Elmalili adds that regular prayer cultivates remorse for major sins. Ibn Ashur allows both prevention and expiation.
  11:114/q13/p3 God turns sins into good deeds after covering and forgiving them. — reasons: Yahya ibn Muadh cites 25:70.
  11:114/q13/p4 Only good can remove evil; an evil deed cannot. — reasons: The Prophet says illicit wealth is not accepted as charity; Abu Abdillah rejects charity and pilgrimage funded by officials' illicit earnings.
  11:114/q13/p5 Inward light from prayer and remembrance dispels darkness from the senses and bodily life. — reasons: Qashani describes prayer's light removing sensory residue. Bursevi compares sacred works nurturing spirit to a watered seed multiplied seven hundredfold (2:261); Wasiti uses the light-and-darkness image.
  11:114/q13/p6 Recent good deeds overtake older sins. — reasons: Hasan urges meeting old sins with new deeds; Abu Ubayda says even vast sins can be overcome by a good deed.
  11:114/q13/p7 Follow a bad deed with a good one as a general moral instruction. — reasons: The Prophet gives this counsel to Muadh and Abu Dharr, alongside fearing God and treating people well.
11:114/q14 Which sins are removed, and on what conditions? [ٱلسَّيِّـَٔاتِ · interpretation] (turns on: How to read the condition about major sins and the scope of divine expiation.)
  11:114/q14/p1 Minor sins are expiated if major sins are avoided. — reasons: The prayer report conditions expiation on avoiding majors. Ibn Ashur cites 53:32 and 4:31. Sunni majority make avoidance a condition of the whole promise, while another group treats majors as excluded from what is erased; Alusi prefers that distinction and argues prayers erase minors even when majors exist.
  11:114/q14/p2 Minor sins require repentance and nonpersistence for erasure. — reasons: Ibn Atiyya invokes sins falling with ablution water and expert legal theorists; Abu Hayyan concurs. Alusi records disagreement and stresses that expiation does not end the duty to repent.
  11:114/q14/p3 Repentance can expiate major sins. — reasons: Jishumi favors Abu Ali's reading; Tabrisi says punishment is cancelled by repentance without dispute. Al-Subki reports debate over whether forgiveness after repentance for sins is certain or presumed.
  11:114/q14/p4 Some good deeds can expiate major as well as minor sins. — reasons: Al-Sadiq says a later good deed can remove a forgotten grave sin. Al-Dhakha'ir cites promises of forgiveness of past and future sins; Ibn al-Mundhir inclines to this. Alusi answers critics who invoke Murji'ism by retaining the duty of repentance.
  11:114/q14/p5 Faith erases unbelief and at least removes eternal punishment, so believers' sins cannot ultimately harm them. — reasons: Razi reports this argument by its proponents.
  11:114/q14/p6 A major sin may be lightened when an expiatory act finds no minor sins. — reasons: Al-Nawawi presents this as a hope.
  11:114/q14/p7 Avoidance of major sins can itself expiate minor sins at each time, when restraint is intentional. — reasons: Al-Balqini reads 4:31 over a lifetime; Alusi rejects that reading with al-Qadi and Ghazali. Ghazali requires ability and desire to commit the major sin.
  11:114/q14/p8 Punishment for minor sins remains possible despite avoidance of majors. — reasons: Alusi reports Sunni authorities citing 4:48 and 18:49; Mu'tazila deny this from 4:31, which may concern unbelief.
11:114/q15 What happened in the incident linked to this verse? [* · reports] (turns on: Whether the reports describe new revelation or application of an existing verse, and the varying details of the man's act and remedy.)
  11:114/q15/p1 A man had illicit physical contact with a woman short of intercourse, confessed, and the Prophet applied the verse and prayer as expiation. — reasons: Accounts vary: a date seller lured a woman home, a man kissed or touched her backside, or a woman by a pool occasioned temptation. Some say the Prophet waited until revelation; others say Gabriel brought it after Asr. Abu Bakr and Umar advised concealment and repentance. Some reports prescribe thorough ablution and two units, others prayer with the Prophet. Tirmidhi grades Ibn Masud's reports hasan sahih, Abu al-Yusr's hasan gharib with a weak transmitter; Ibn Ashur says Muadh and Abu al-Yusr routes are weak. Ibn Abi Hatim and Durr preserve other versions.
  11:114/q15/p2 The pool encounter ended in remorse, with forgiveness sought and four prayer units prescribed. — reasons: Ibn Kathir calls Yahya ibn Ja'da's account mursal. The reports differ on whether the man found a woman by a pool or approached her while she bathed, and whether impotence stopped him.
  11:114/q15/p3 The verse already existed, and the Prophet applied its general rule to the penitent. — reasons: Ibn Ashur cites a Tirmidhi transmission saying the Prophet recited the verse without saying it newly descended; 'revealed' can mean applied to the case.
  11:114/q15/p4 The verse was newly revealed in response to the confession. — reasons: The Prophet's silence or delay until revelation is a recurrent detail; Ibn Ashur notes this wording would make the verse Medinan.
11:114/q16 Who was the man in the confession report? [* · reports] (turns on: Variant transmission of the man's name, kunya, and tribe.)
  11:114/q16/p1 Abu al-Yusr, the Ansari date seller; names given include Amr ibn Ghaziya and Ka'b ibn Amr. — reasons: Mawardi, Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn Kathir preserve divergent personal names for Abu al-Yusr. Tirmidhi's Abu al-Yusr transmission is reported as hasan gharib, with Qays ibn al-Rabi weakened.
  11:114/q16/p2 Abu Miqbal or Abu Nufayl, Amir ibn Qays al-Ansari. — reasons: Muqatil gives Abu Miqbal Amir ibn Qays of Banu al-Najjar; Ibn Kathir quotes Abu Nufayl as a variant.
  11:114/q16/p3 An Ansari named Flan ibn Muattib or Ibn Muqib. — reasons: Ibrahim's reports supply these differing forms.
  11:114/q16/p4 A man of Banu Ghanm or Banu Tamim. — reasons: Yazid ibn Ruman's transmitted tribal designations vary.
  11:114/q16/p5 Nabhan al-Tammar. — reasons: Abu Hayyan reports this identification for the good-deeds clause.
  11:114/q16/p6 An Ansari called Abbad. — reasons: Reported as an alternative identification.
  11:114/q16/p7 The report leaves the man unnamed. — reasons: These accounts describe his conduct without a name.
11:114/q17 To whom did the Prophet say the verse's remedy applies? [إِنَّ ٱلْحَسَنَٰتِ يُذْهِبْنَ ٱلسَّيِّـَٔاتِ · law]
  11:114/q17/p1 It applies generally to all believers or the Prophet's community who act on it. — reasons: The questioner is variously Umar, Muadh, or Abu al-Yusr (Ibn al-Jawzi). The Prophet's answers uniformly make the remedy general; al-Alusi says the occasion does not restrict the wording.
11:114/q18 What legal consequence follows for an unlawful kiss or touch? [إِنَّ ٱلْحَسَنَٰتِ يُذْهِبْنَ ٱلسَّيِّـَٔاتِ · law]
  11:114/q18/p1 It does not incur the fixed penalty for intercourse. — reasons: Qurtubi infers this from the incident and expiation through prayer.
  11:114/q18/p2 Even a man and woman found in one garment incur neither a fixed penalty nor discretionary punishment. — reasons: Ibn al-Mundhir is reported to choose this on the basis of the incident.
11:114/q19 What is the grammatic

al form of ذكرى? [ذِكْرَىٰ · grammar]
  11:114/q19/p1 It is a verbal noun ending in feminine alif, with other attested forms and a plural. — reasons: Abu Ali compares العدوى, الدعوى and شورى; Sibawayh records الذكر with dal and cites Ibn Muqbil's line, alongside 12:45. Qurtubi calls it a verbal noun.
11:114/q20 To what does ذلك point? [ذَٰلِكَ · referent] (turns on: Which antecedent the demonstrative resumes.)
  11:114/q20/p1 The preceding counsel and commands, including steadfastness and prayer. — reasons: Kashshaf starts at the uprightness command; Tabari includes this surah's commands and prohibitions. Ibn Atiyya and Ibn al-Jawzi mention avoiding transgression and unjust rulers; Biqai includes warning and consolation.
  11:114/q20/p2 The command to establish prayer at these times. — reasons: Abu Hayyan prefers the nearest antecedent; Ibn Atiyya says prayer supplies a cause and setting for remembrance.
  11:114/q20/p3 The statement or promise that good deeds erase sins. — reasons: Ibn Atiyya says this encourages good deeds; Jishumi calls it the promise itself.
  11:114/q20/p4 The Qur'an. — reasons: Wahidi says it is an admonition for one who remembers the Quran.
  11:114/q20/p5 This, meaning the present admonition. — reasons: Ibn Abbas takes ذلك in the sense of هذا.
11:114/q21 Who benefits from the reminder, and what kind of reminder is it? [ذِكْرَىٰ لِلذَّٰكِرِينَ · interpretation] (turns on: Whether the reminder is admonition, repentance, doctrinal strengthening, or inward recollection.)
  11:114/q21/p1 It is admonition for people who remember God and heed it. — reasons: Tabari contrasts responsive people with sealed hearts and mentions hope for reward and fear of warning. Hasan describes remembering in prosperity, adversity, health and illness; Mujahid adds standing, sitting and lying. Alusi and Qurtubi say those who heed are named because they benefit.
  11:114/q21/p2 It is a call to repentance or recollection of one's own sin. — reasons: Al-Kalbi calls it repentance; Yazid ibn Ruman and Ibn Jurayj say the penitent man continued to remember his deed.
  11:114/q21/p3 It strengthens believers in religion. — reasons: Abu Muslim explains the reminder's effect this way.
  11:114/q21/p4 It recalls spiritual clarity, gathered attention, intimacy and taste. — reasons: Both connect prayer times and sins' removal to inward recollection.
11:114/q22 How does the verse connect to nearby commands and other verses? [* · links]
  11:114/q22/p1 Prayer follows the command to remain upright as the foremost aid to steadfastness, and its expiatory power explains the command. — reasons: Ibn Ashur says 'indeed' emphasizes the causal explanation and links 29:45; Biqai says prayer cures the weakness behind lesser sins.
  11:114/q22/p2 Other verses supply or parallel these prayer times. — reasons: Muqatil recalls Moses' prayer for remembrance at 20:14; Hasan invokes 17:78; Razi and Elmalili cite 20:130; Bursevi adds 50:39–40. Study Quran compares disagreement over the middle prayer at 2:238.
  11:114/q22/p3 The verse's direct address to the Prophet marks positive commands, while prohibitions address the community. — reasons: Elmalili says this shift implies transgression and inclination to oppressors are conceivable for the community, not the Prophet.
11:114/q23 Was this verse revealed in Mecca or Medina? [* · sciences] (turns on: Whether 'revealed' in the confession account denotes first revelation or application of an earlier verse.)
  11:114/q23/p1 It was revealed in Medina as an exception within the surah. — reasons: Ibn Abbas and Qatada infer this from the confession report's 'revealed to him' wording; many commentators list verses 12, 17 and 114 as possible exceptions.
  11:114/q23/p2 It is Meccan along with the whole surah; the Prophet later applied it to the penitent. — reasons: Rashid Rida rejects Medina dating as unconvincing. Ibn Kathir suggests it may predate the five prayers of the Night Journey, when two daily prayers and night vigil were required.
  11:114/q23/p3 If newly revealed in Medina, it was placed here for coherence with steadfastness and patience. — reasons: Ibn Ashur points to the adjacent commands at 11:112 and 11:115.
11:114/q24 What distinct reports illustrate the verse's hope and expiation? [* · reports]
  11:114/q24/p1 The five prayers wash away sins like repeated bathing in a river or leaves falling from a branch. — reasons: Salman shakes a dry branch; the Prophet's river image asks whether dirt could remain after five baths. Tabatabai lists parallel Sunni transmissions.
  11:114/q24/p2 It is the most hopeful verse, according to a report from Ali and the Prophet. — reasons: Ali rejects proposed alternatives at 4:48 and 4:110 before identifying this prayer command.
  11:114/q24/p3 God's mercy to a believer exceeds a mother bird's care for her chick. — reasons: The Prophet uses the bird's entrusted chick as the comparison.
  11:114/q24/p4 A worshiper who makes people despair of mercy is himself made to despair after death. — reasons: Zayd ibn Aslam transmits the warning.
  11:114/q24/p5 Ablution itself purifies and draws immense reward. — reasons: Bursevi notes jurists who treated used ablution cloth as impure because sins wash off; the Moses report promises a garden per drop, and Hafiz praises prayer purified by tears.
  11:114/q24/p6 Faith and lawful deeds matter: illicit wealth is not blessed or accepted as charity. — reasons: The Prophet says faith is given to those God loves and requires a surrendered heart and tongue and a safe neighbor.
  11:114/q24/p7 Testimony of faith can erase sins, though some specific routes are weak or unique. — reasons: Ibn Kathir notes Uthman al-Waqqasi is weak in one Anas route and another route is unique through Mastur.
  11:114/q24/p8 Every deed is recorded, so one should not belittle a sin or a good deed. — reasons: Al-Sadiq warns of angels recording public and hidden acts.
11:114/q25 What inward reading does the verse support? [* · inward]
  11:114/q25/p1 Prayer and remembrance bring light that clears sensory darkness and sustains presence. — reasons: Qashani relates five prayers to five senses and night vigil to refining natural powers; Bursevi describes the luminous spirit nourished by good works, and Wasiti contrasts obedience's light with sin's darkness. The Study Quran reports a heart polished by remembrance (13:28).

## THE NEW NOTES
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالجزاء)#481/r10] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Poetry can postpone a present-tense conditional clause after its answer, as in Jarir's line and the saying about the man who meets bribes.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالجزاء)#481/r5] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | A nominal clause such as إن تأتني أنا كريم cannot normally answer a conditional, since it begins independently rather than attaching to what precedes.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالجزاء)#481/r6] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Poets may use an independent nominal answer under necessity; Sībawayh cites lines by Hassan ibn Thabit and al-Asadi as examples.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالجزاء)#481/r7] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | إن تأتني لأفعلن is normally unsuitable because the oath lām clause begins independently; with لئن, the oath lām may be understood or stated.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالجزاء)#481/r9] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | A past-tense condition can follow its answer, as in Zuhayr's line; reversing a present-tense إن clause is normally disfavored because إن governs the verb.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p418/r1] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | Al-Wahidi says he heard Abu al-Abbas al-Asamm and transmitted from him; Abu Bakr al-Khwarizmi appointed him to teach his lesson during his absence.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p418/r2] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | Al-Wahidi notes that he wrote major works and critical supplements addressing leading scholars of language and grammar.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p418/r3] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | He studied intensively with al-Thaʿlabi for years, visiting daily to hear, read, annotate, memorize, research and discuss while working through poetry collections and language books.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p418/r4] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | Al-Thaʿlabi urged him to devote himself to Quran commentary; al-Wahidi replied that literary study prepared him for tafsir and continued visiting until death separated them.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p418/r5] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | As a young man he studied under Abu al-Hasan al-Darir, whom he describes as outstanding in subtle grammar and the intricacies of Arabic, and devoted to training him.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p418/r6] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | Under al-Darir, al-Wahidi studied grammar, morphology and semantics, compiled nearly one hundred fascicles on difficult issues, heard works on grammar, metrics and linguistic causes, and received his book on Ibn Mihran's qiraat justifications.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p418/r7] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | He studied with Abu al-Hasan Imran al-Maghribi al-Maliki, whom he calls unmatched in i'rab, and says he absorbed the finest of his knowledge during his stay.
[JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p158/r1] JURJANI-ASRAR, d. 471 · author | holds | Al-Ṣanawbarī likens stretched arcs on a pond to extended eyebrows: stretching reduces their curvature, just as extending an eyebrow does.
[JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p158/r2] JURJANI-ASRAR, d. 471 · author | reports | Ibn al-Muʿtazz compares early raindrops on earth to hurried dots scattered across a book page, combining shape with movement.
[JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p158/r3] JURJANI-ASRAR, d. 471 · author | holds | Motion becomes a composite image when parts move in different directions; a wheel or arrow moves simply, while a page alternately closing and opening changes direction.
[JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p158/r4] JURJANI-ASRAR, d. 471 · author | holds | Al-Aʿshā compares a ship tossed by waves to a young calf's irregular rising and falling; الرباح can mean a calf or, by another view, a monkey, and الكرع is rainwater.
[JURJANI-ASRAR

:v1p181/r1] JURJANI-ASRAR, d. 471 · author | holds | Poets compare a dark horse's bright forehead to a star or dawn and its body to night; Ibn al-Muʿtazz reverses the image, making dawn a horse's blaze.
[JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p181/r2] JURJANI-ASRAR, d. 471 · author | holds | Though comparing maidens' figures to cypresses is conventional, poets refresh the image by making cypresses resemble women; a poem also depicts trees leaning as if seeking an embrace.
[JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p181/r3] JURJANI-ASRAR, d. 471 · author | holds | In Ibn al-Muʿtazz's cypress image, branches first lean toward an embrace and then recoil; the return to uprightness is faster than the initial bend.
[JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p181/r4] JURJANI-ASRAR, d. 471 · author | holds | A shy person withdraws faster than approaching; fear and embarrassment impel more strongly than hope, while approach allows deliberation and withdrawal is compelled.
[JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p181/r5] JURJANI-ASRAR, d. 471 · author | reports | Ibn al-Muʿtazz figures festivity and delight through women, presenting wine circulated among companions in the hand of a lovely woman.
[JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p183/r1] JURJANI-ASRAR, d. 471 · author | holds | Poets compare young women's breasts to pomegranates, and also reverse the comparison to describe a pomegranate as a maiden's breast.
[JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p183/r2] JURJANI-ASRAR, d. 471 · author | holds | Clear streams resemble swords in the water's whiteness and gleam and in their elongated shape; poets also reverse the image, likening swords' strokes to streams.
[JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p191/r1] JURJANI-ASRAR, d. 471 · author | holds | Ibn al-Muʿtazz requires the bird to be clipped-winged: a fixed tent buffeted inside by wind moves like a bird whose restricted wings beat continuously and backward.
[JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p191/r2] JURJANI-ASRAR, d. 471 · author | holds | A comparison cannot always be reversed: when one object is an established extreme in a quality, it serves as the measure for an uncertain object, not vice versa.
[JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p191/r3] JURJANI-ASRAR, d. 471 · author | rejects | Al-Buḥturī's night-as-ink comparison is weak because ink is not an unsurpassed standard of blackness; the night itself is the better established measure.
[JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p247/r1] JURJANI-ASRAR, d. 471 · author | holds | Ibn al-Muʿtazz first compares the rose's redness to blushing, then imagines literal shame and invents its cause: the rose feels unworthy beside the superior narcissus.
[JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p247/r2] JURJANI-ASRAR, d. 471 · author | reports | Abū Hilāl al-ʿAskarī imagines the violet boasting that it matches a maiden's cheek; asking its back exposes the claim and comically elevates the flower's status.
[JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p149/r1] JURJANI-DALAIL, d. 471 · author | holds | With two definite nouns under kāna, either may be called subject and the other predicate; this grammatical choice does not make all reversed clauses equivalent.
[JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p149/r2] JURJANI-DALAIL, d. 471 · author | holds | Fronting can set exclusive focus; reversing “only musk is perfume” and related lines by Jarir and al-Mutanabbi changes the intended meaning.
[DAMGHANI:v1p255/r7] DAMGHANI, d. 478 · author | holds | Sayyiʾāt can mean minor sins that good deeds remove; another verse speaks of overlooking them. | mentions 46:16
[DAMGHANI:v1p293/r4] DAMGHANI, d. 478 · author | holds | Aṭrāf al-nahār means times at the ends of the day; for 11:114 the work gives dawn, noon, and afternoon, also noting dawn prayer. | mentions 20:130
[IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p362/r1] IBNJAWZI-NUZHA, d. 597 · author | holds | Al-sayyiʾāt are the opposite of good deeds.
[IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p362/r2] IBNJAWZI-NUZHA, d. 597 · أهل التفسير | reports | One Qur'anic sense is associating partners with God. | mentions 4:18, 10:27
[IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p362/r3] IBNJAWZI-NUZHA, d. 597 · أهل التفسير | reports | A second sense is punishment or the consequences of wrongdoing. | mentions 39:51
[IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p362/r4] IBNJAWZI-NUZHA, d. 597 · أهل التفسير | reports | A third sense is harm or misfortune, including the afflictions that pass away. | mentions 7:168, 11:10
[IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p362/r5] IBNJAWZI-NUZHA, d. 597 · أهل التفسير | reports | A fourth sense is evil or wicked schemes. | mentions 40:45
[IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p362/r6] IBNJAWZI-NUZHA, d. 597 · أهل التفسير | reports | A fifth sense is men having sex with men, as in the account of Lot's people. | mentions 11:78
[RAZI-FULL:v1p25/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Al-Rāzī treats applying “lafẓ” to sounds and letters as metaphorical: breath is expelled from the chest; it causes the words and makes their production resemble casting them outward.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p25/r10] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Under ب ع ر, البعر is linked to movement from the inside to the outside.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p25/r11] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Under ر ع ب, fear is called رعب because a person shifts from one state to another when it occurs.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p25/r12] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Under ر ب ع, الربع is a place people move from and to.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p25/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | All six permutations of the root ع ب ر signify crossing or transition.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p25/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Under ع ب ر, “expression” involves moving from letter to letter and transferring meaning from the speaker’s mind to the listener.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p25/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Under ع ب ر, العبرة is a tear moving from inside the eye outward, while العبر denotes crossing from the witnessed to the unseen.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p25/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The word معبر denotes a crossing because a person passes by it from one side of the sea to the other.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p25/r6] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The word التعبير denotes moving from what one sees in a dream to hidden meanings.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p25/r7] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Under ع ر ب, Arabs are so named for their frequent movements on the winter and summer journeys.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p25/r8] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Under ع ر ب, iʿrāb moves an utterance from obscurity before inflection to knowledge and clarity after inflection.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p25/r9] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Under ب ر ع, برع means becoming complete and increasing.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p48/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Short vowels are parts of the long-vowel letters: those letters admit increase and decrease, their lower limit is the short vowels, and lengthening a short vowel yields a long vowel; usage also favors substituting a part for its whole.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p48/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | Some hold that beginning with a vowelless consonant is impossible because a vowel sound follows articulation of the consonant; others permit it.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p48/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The ḍamma is the heaviest vowel, requiring both lips and two muscles; kasra needs one muscle, while fatḥa requires only a slight effort, as anatomy and experience show.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p48/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Vowel coloring varies by regional constitution: Azerbaijanis tend to color their words with ḍamma, while many regions tend toward kasra.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p48/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | When the three vowels and sukūn are inflectional, they are called nominative, accusative, genitive or lowered, and jussive; when structural, they are called fatḥ, ḍamm, kasr, and pause.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p48/r6] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · قطرب | reports | Quṭrub holds that structural vowels are like inflectional vowels.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p48/r7] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Al-Rāzī calls the dispute verbal: the vowels are perceptually identical in essence, but they are not equally warranted by differing grammatical governors.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p65/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · أهل السنة والجماعة | holds | Ahl al-Sunna argue that if human capacity is directed to only one alternative, compulsion follows; if it can support both, preference needs a determinant, whose agent either repeats the dilemma or makes action necessary or impossible.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p65/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · أهل السنة والجماعة | holds | They reject uncaused preference: it would undermine inference from a possible outcome’s preference to a determinant and leave the act as chance, not the servant’s doing, returning to sheer compulsion.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p65/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · أهل السنة والجماعة | holds | They argue that an act contrary to God’s knowledge would turn divine knowledge into ignorance; the same objection raised against predestination therefore applies to foreknowledge.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p65/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · أهل السنة والجماعة | holds | They argue that seeking refuge from Satan refutes predestination: if it asks God to prevent temptation by warning, that prevention has already occurred; if by coercion, it conflicts with the jinn’s accountability.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p65/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · المعتزلة | reports | The Muʿtazilites reply that seeking refuge asks for divine graces that encourage the accountable person to do good and avoid evil; some graces are fitting only after the supplication.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p65/r6] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · أهل السنة والجماعة | holds | Ahl al-Sunna answer that if such graces tip the balance toward action, the action becomes necessary and undercuts Muʿtazilite freedom; if they do not, they have no effect and are futile.
[BURHAN:v1p196/r2] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | reports | The Hūd verse is reported as revealed concerning Abū Miqbal al-Ḥusayn ibn ʿUmar ibn Qays and a woman who bought dates from him, whom he tried to seduce.
[BURHAN:v1p29/r1] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | An ayah may descend twice to magnify its importance and recall it when a new cause arises; the Fatiha is said to have descended once in Mecca and once in Medina, and this resolves the report about the Makkan Hūd verse.
[BURHAN:v1p29/r2] BURHAN, d. 794 · ابن مسعود | reports | In a report in both Ṣaḥīḥs, a man who had kissed a woma

n told the Prophet, and this verse was revealed; the Prophet said it applies to the whole community. Al-Tirmidhi or another source identifies the man as Abū al-Yusr.
[BURHAN:v1p29/r6] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | A new question or incident can prompt the Prophet to receive an ayah that had already descended; its repetition reminds people of the text and shows that it encompasses the new event's ruling.
[NASHR:v1p206/r1] NASHR, d. 833 · أبو عمرو الداني | reports | A report says the Prophet recited in taḥqīq through the transmission given by the author; al-Dānī calls it rare and known only by this route, but with a sound chain.
[NASHR:v1p206/r2] NASHR, d. 833 · أبو عمرو الداني | reports | Al-Dānī calls the report a major basis for the duty to practice taḥqīq and learn precision and tajwīd, citing its connected chain and reliable transmitters.
[NASHR:v1p206/r3] NASHR, d. 833 · author | holds | Ḥadr derives from “descending quickly” and means a rapid, compressed recitation using reported shortening, stilling, ikhtilās, substitution, large assimilation, and eased hamza while preserving connection, inflection, and clear letter production; it opposes taḥqīq.
[NASHR:v1p206/r4] NASHR, d. 833 · author | holds | Ḥadr can increase recitation's reward, but must not truncate madd, erase ghunna, overly shorten vowels, invalidate recitation, or leave the bounds of tartīl.
[NASHR:v1p206/r5] NASHR, d. 833 · عبد الله بن مسعود | reports | A man told Ibn Masʿūd he had recited the Mufaṣṣal in one rakʿa; Ibn Masʿūd rebuked this as reciting like poetry, in a report cited from Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī.
[NASHR:v1p206/r6] NASHR, d. 833 · author | holds | Ḥadr is associated with Ibn Kathīr, Abū Jaʿfar, and readers who shorten the separated madd, including Abū ʿAmr, Yaʿqūb, Qālūn, al-Aṣbahānī from Warsh, al-Walī from Ḥafṣ, and most Iraqi transmitters from al-Ḥulwānī from Hishām.
[NASHR:v1p288/r1] NASHR, d. 833 · author | holds | In the large-idghām inventory, assimilation before jīm has seventeen cases, including الصالحات جناح; before dhāl there are nine, including السيئات ذلك and الآخرة ذلك.
[NASHR:v1p288/r11] NASHR, d. 833 · ابن حبش | reports | Ibn Ḥabash alone reports that al-Sūsī clearly articulates الصلاة طرفي النهار because the vowel is light and the preceding consonant is still; other performance authorities assimilate for homorganicity and the strength of ṭāʾ.
[NASHR:v1p288/r9] NASHR, d. 833 · author | reports | Three ṭāʾ environments are listed; in ولتأت طائفة, readers who assimilate other jussives assimilate, while those who articulate them clearly do so here, though homorganicity and the strong ṭāʾ favor assimilation. Al-Dānī and most accept both.
[NASHR:v2p291/r5] NASHR, d. 833 · أبو جعفر | reports | Abū Jaʿfar, Ṭalḥa, Shayba, ʿĪsā ibn ʿAmr, and named transmitters from Abū ʿAmr read زلفا with ḍamma on lām; the others read it with fatḥa.
[NASHR:v2p291/r6] NASHR, d. 833 · author | holds | Both vowels are attested dialects in the plural of زلفة, meaning a portion of the early night, as in ظُلَم/ظلمة and يُسْر/يُسْرة.
[ITQAN:v1p104/r5] ITQAN, d. 911 · الزركشي | reports | Al-Zarkashī says revelation may recur to magnify a verse, renew its reminder when its occasion arises, and prevent its being forgotten; he cites 11:114. | mentions 17:85
[ITQAN:v1p104/r6] ITQAN, d. 911 · الزركشي | holds | Al-Zarkashī resolves the apparent clash between the Meccan status of al-Isrāʾ and Hūd and Medinan reports about their occasions by saying the verses descended twice.
[ITQAN:v1p251/r1] ITQAN, d. 911 · author | holds | Large assimilation covers sixteen letters, under mnemonic رض سنشد حجتك بذل قثم; the first consonant must not be geminated, tanwīn, or a pronoun tāʾ.
[ITQAN:v1p251/r3] ITQAN, d. 911 · author | holds | Tāʾ assimilates into ten following letters, including ṭāʾ in the phrase about prayer at the two ends of the day.
[ITQAN:v1p251/r5] ITQAN, d. 911 · author | holds | Thāʾ assimilates into five letters; jīm into shīn and tāʾ; and ḥāʾ into ʿayn only in زحزح عن النار. | mentions 2:223, 2:223, 27:16
[ITQAN:v1p48/r1] ITQAN, d. 911 · author | holds | Three verses are excepted from the classification of Hūd as Meccan, including the command to pray at the two ends of the day.
[ITQAN:v1p48/r2] ITQAN, d. 911 · author | holds | The author supports the Medinan classification of the third exception with sound reports through several routes, saying it concerned Abū al-Yusr.
[ITQAN:v3p107/r1] ITQAN, d. 911 · الكواشي | reports | Al-Kawāshī says an imperative used like a declarative is more emphatic because it conveys obligation, as in the example of promising hospitality.
[ITQAN:v3p107/r2] ITQAN, d. 911 · ابن عبد السلام | reports | Ibn ʿAbd al-Salām explains the force of this construction by the imperative's sense of obligation, transferred to the declarative.
[ITQAN:v3p116/r1] ITQAN, d. 911 · author | holds | The fragment compares trying to keep water in a cupped hand, which leaves nothing, to the elusive nature of worldly life.
[ITQAN:v3p146/r1] ITQAN, d. 911 · الشيخ بهاء الدين | reports | Bahāʾ al-Dīn distinguishes ellipsis, where a short expression is part of a longer one, from concision, where few words convey a longer meaning.
[ITQAN:v3p146/r2] ITQAN, d. 911 · بعضهم | reports | Some define concision as multiplying meaning while reducing wording; another defines it as using fewer words than customary for the meaning.
[ITQAN:v3p146/r3] ITQAN, d. 911 · author | holds | Concision is eloquent because it demonstrates mastery of expression, as the Prophet's saying that he was given comprehensive speech illustrates.
[ITQAN:v3p65#2/r1] ITQAN, d. 911 · ابن الحصار | holds | Ibn al-Ḥiṣār requires an explicit transmission from the Prophet or a Companion stating that one verse abrogated another to establish abrogation.
[ITQAN:v3p65#2/r2] ITQAN, d. 911 · ابن الحصار | holds | Ibn al-Ḥiṣār also allows abrogation to be inferred from certain chronology when a definite contradiction requires identifying which ruling came first.
[ITQAN:v3p65#2/r3] ITQAN, d. 911 · ابن الحصار | rejects | Ibn al-Ḥiṣār rejects claims based only on lay commentators or independent juristic reasoning without reliable transmission and clear contradiction; abrogation depends on transmission and chronology, not opinion.
[ITQAN:v3p65#2/r4] ITQAN, d. 911 · ابن الحصار | rejects | Ibn al-Ḥiṣār rejects both extremes: refusing sound solitary reports altogether and accepting a commentator's or jurist's claim without evidence.
[ITQAN:v3p65#2/r5] ITQAN, d. 911 · صاحب الفنون | reports | For abrogation of recitation while retaining the ruling, Ṣāḥib al-Funūn says the wisdom is to show the community's readiness to obey on probable evidence, like Abraham's response to his dream. | mentions 37:102
[ITQAN:v3p65#2/r6] ITQAN, d. 911 · ابن عمر | reports | Ibn ʿUmar warns against claiming to possess the whole Qur'an because much of it has gone, advising people to say they have what remains apparent.
[ITQAN:v4p514#2/r2] ITQAN, d. 911 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | A weak report from Ibn ʿAbbās says the Prophet called a new good deed after an old sin unusually quick and effective in seeking and reaching its goal.
[ITQAN:v4p514#2/r3] ITQAN, d. 911 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | Abū Dharr reports that the Prophet advised following a bad deed with a good one to erase it, and identified lā ilāha illā Allāh as the best good deed.
[SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p987/r1] SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT · author | holds | Zulfa means drawing nearer gradually; in the verse it broadly conveys nearness and drawing close.
[SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p987/r2] SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT · كثير من المفسرين | reports | Many commentators understand the near portions of night as the prayers closest to daytime, namely Maghrib and ʿIshāʾ.
[SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p987/r3] SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT · بعضهم | reports | Some interpret it as drawing near to God through night prayer, without restricting it to Maghrib and ʿIshāʾ.
[SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p987/r4] SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT · author | holds | He concludes that zulfa carries the general sense of drawing near.

item.text: Most new notes address existing questions, but a large set discusses unrelated grammar, rhetoric, biography, or recitation in general. I’ll keep those separate from the verse interpretations so they don’t appear to support claims they never make.

The [updated map](/Volumes/aro/projects/prose_generation/enrichment/v9/work/map-103_1-20261008/map/out/sol-high/11-114.u1.raw.jsonl) has **15 additions to existing positions, 4 new positions, and 4 new questions**. The checker returned `OK`.
